Uprightness
UP-rite-nes
n.
From upright (Old English upriht, “straight up”) + -ness. Renders the Hebrew yōsher, “straightness, uprightness,” from yāshar, “to be straight, level,” and the Greek euthutēs, “straightness.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Uprightness is the moral quality of being straight before God—a life lived along the line of what is right, true, and just, without crookedness, deceit, or deviation. The Hebrew imagery is geometric: the upright life is the straight line, the plumb-line standard, the road that does not bend. The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them; he that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known; the just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him. Job is described by God Himself as a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil. David prays in his coronation, I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way... I will walk within my house with a perfect heart; and again, let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee. The Psalter’s great word for the people of God is the upright: the upright shall dwell in thy presence; good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way; light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. Uprightness is not sinless perfection—Scripture never claims that for any but Christ—but it is the settled direction of the life: the heart aimed straight at God, the conscience kept sensitive, the path corrected when it bends, the integrity that aligns the inward and outward man so that what the believer is in private and what he is in public are the same man. The upright life is therefore the practical fruit of the heart made new by the gospel: regeneration produces a new direction, and the new direction is straightness—the long arc of a life lived under God’s eye, in the plumb-line of His revealed will, with the integrity that makes the believer a single man before God and his neighbor and not a double-souled creature whose private life contradicts his public profession.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines UPRIGHTNESS as perpendicular erection; in morals, integrity in principle or practice; honesty; rectitude of mind and conduct; freedom from deceit or perversity.

expand to see more

UPRIGHTNESS, n. — 1. Perpendicular erection. 2. In morals, integrity in principle or practice; honesty; rectitude of mind and conduct; freedom from deceit or perversity. Let integrity and uprightness preserve me (Psa 25:21). 3. Honesty; consistent and straightforward dealing; opposed to deceit, fraud, and crookedness.

UPRIGHT, a. — 1. Erect; perpendicular to the plane of the horizon. 2. Adhering to rectitude in all social intercourse; not deviating from correct moral principles; honest; just; pure.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 25:21 — "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee."

Proverbs 10:9 — "He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known."

Job 1:8 — "And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?"

Psalm 97:11 — "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Uprightness is corrupted by the double-life pattern of the present age in which the public profession and the private practice are different lives entirely—and by the brittle moralism that mistakes external scrupulosity for the inward integrity that aligns the whole man before God.

expand to see more

The double-life pattern is the most common contemporary corruption of uprightness. The believer maintains the public profession of faith—present at services, present in conversation, present in the categories of self-identification—while the private life (the screen-history, the inward thought-life, the secret habits, the relationships hidden from oversight) tells a different story. The two lives never integrate. The inward and outward man are different men. Uprightness as Scripture means it is the precise opposite: the integrity that aligns the inward and outward, so that what the believer is in private and what he is in public are the same man. The recovery is not better performance of the public life but the bringing of the private life into the light: confession to a brother, accountability, the deliberate work of integrating what has been split. The upright man walks surely because his life is one piece; the double man, even when his public life is impressive, walks unsurely because the foundations are riven.

The opposite corruption is brittle moralism—the external scrupulosity that mistakes itself for uprightness while the heart is unchanged. The Pharisees were the textbook case: outwardly meticulous about every fringe and tithe and ceremonial detail, inwardly full of extortion and excess, whitewashed sepulchers beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within. The Christ who diagnoses them sets the contrast: the upright man is upright at the level of the heart first, with the outward life flowing as the proper fruit of the inward, not painted on as the substitute for it. Recover the inward primacy, and uprightness recovers its substance: a heart aimed straight at God by the regenerating Spirit, with the outward life lived consistently along that aim, in a single integrity that is the long arc of a life lived under God’s eye and pleasing in His sight.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yōsher (straightness, uprightness) and yāshar (to be straight, level); Greek euthutēs (straightness)—the moral straightness of the heart-aimed life, integrating the inward and outward man into a single integrity before God.

expand to see more

Hebrew yōsher (H3476) — straightness, uprightness (Job 33:23; Ps 25:21; Prov 2:13; Eccl 12:10).

Hebrew yāshar (H3477, adj.) — straight, right, upright; the great Old Testament moral adjective.

Hebrew yāshar (H3474, vb.) — to be straight, level, right.

Greek euthutēs (G2118) — straightness; Heb 1:8 of the scepter of God’s kingdom.

Usage

"He that walketh uprightly walketh surely—integrity gives the surefooted gait that the double life can never sustain."

"Uprightness is not sinless perfection but the settled direction of the life: the heart aimed straight at God, with the inward and outward man integrated into a single integrity."

"Double-life pattern and brittle moralism are opposite corruptions; biblical uprightness is heart-deep and life-wide, the long arc of a man living under God’s eye."
